subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: One postulate of special relativity is that the speed of light in a vacuum is:
options: The same for all inertial observers
questions.explain: The constancy of c for all inertial frames is central to special relativity.

questions.q: The other postulate is that the laws of physics are:
options: The same in all inertial reference frames
questions.explain: No inertial frame is preferred.

questions.q: An inertial reference frame:
questions.explain: Inertial frames move at constant velocity relative to one another.

questions.q: Time dilation means a clock moving relative to an observer runs:
options: Slower than the observer's own clock
questions.explain: Moving clocks tick slower (t = gamma x t0).

questions.q: Length contraction means a fast-moving object is measured to be:
options: Shorter along its direction of motion
questions.explain: Contraction occurs only along the direction of motion (L = L0/gamma).

questions.q: The Lorentz factor gamma increases as speed:
questions.explain: gamma = 1/sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) grows without limit as v approaches c.

questions.q: At everyday speeds (v much less than c), gamma is approximately:
questions.explain: Relativistic effects are negligible at low speed.

questions.q: Proper time is measured:
options: In the frame where the two events occur at the same location
questions.explain: Proper time is the shortest measured interval.

questions.q: A ship travels at 0.6c (gamma = 1.25). A 10-year trip in the ship's frame is, in Earth's frame:
questions.explain: Earth time = gamma x proper time = 1.25 x 10 = 12.5 years.

questions.q: Two events simultaneous in one inertial frame:
options: May not be simultaneous in another moving frame
questions.explain: Simultaneity is relative to the observer's frame.

questions.q: More atmospheric muons reach the ground than expected classically because, in Earth's frame:
options: Their decay time is dilated (they live longer)
questions.explain: Time dilation extends their measured lifetime (length contraction in the muon frame).

questions.q: Simple velocity addition fails near light speed because:
options: Nothing can exceed the speed of light
Velocities add to more than c
questions.explain: Relativistic velocity addition keeps the result below c.

questions.q: Space and time in special relativity are treated as:
questions.explain: Measurements of space and time are frame-dependent.

questions.q: As speed approaches c, the energy needed to accelerate a massive object further:
questions.explain: This is why a massive object cannot reach c.

questions.q: Proper length is measured:
options: In the frame where the object is at rest
questions.explain: Proper length is the maximum (rest-frame) length.

questions.q: An accelerating frame is described as:
questions.explain: Special relativity's postulates apply to inertial frames.

questions.q: If gamma = 2, a proper time of 5.0 microseconds appears in the lab as:
questions.explain: Dilated time = gamma x proper time = 2 x 5.0 = 10 microseconds.

questions.q: Time dilation and length contraction are:
options: Real, symmetric effects each observer measures of the other
questions.explain: Each inertial observer measures the other's clocks slow and lengths contracted.

questions.q: Why are relativistic effects unnoticed in daily life?
options: Everyday speeds are tiny compared with c
Light is too fast to see
questions.explain: gamma is essentially 1 at ordinary speeds.

questions.q: A rod of proper length 10 m moves with gamma = 2. Its measured length is:
questions.explain: Contracted length = L0/gamma = 10/2 = 5.0 m.
